metadata.title: White House blocks Politico from Air Force One

sources.news_title: POLITICO Blocked From Air Force One Amid Battle Over Media Access
sources.text:
The White House on Monday blocked POLITICO from boarding Air Force One and carrying out its print pool duties, marking the latest escalation in an ongoing battle over media outlets’ access to President Donald Trump.
“The White House has blocked today's print pooler, Politico, from traveling on Air Force One,” Washington Post reporter Katherine Doyle wrote in a White House pool report Monday afternoon.
Doyle added that “since [the White House] was unable to find a replacement, there is no primary print pooler on this trip,” and noted that she would be making reports as “the secondary pooler” as Trump travels to Nebraska for a campaign rally ahead of the midterms.
CBS, the designated representative for the TV pool on Monday, is also sharing its notes with news organizations during the trip. “Neither news organization is replacing Politico,” Josh Gross of CBS News emphasized in an email.
“Many outlets including POLITICO are granted access to attend and cover presidential events unilaterally, but traveling with the President of the United States aboard Air Force One is a privilege not a right,” a White House official tells TIME. The official adds that Trump is “the most accessible President in American history,” and says that he will “continue to grant an unprecedented level of access to the press.”
A spokesperson for POLITICO confirmed to TIME that the outlet was blocked from Monday's out-of-town travel pool.
In the White House pool system, a rotating group of journalists accompanies the President to various events and shares updates with the wider press corps to enable news organizations to widely provide coverage despite the often limited space at event venues or on board Air Force One.
But that pool coverage of Trump has been complicated by the President’s most recent efforts to punish media organizations whose coverage he objects to.
POLITICO is one of three outlets, also including CNN and MS NOW, that Trump announced that he was banning from the White House on Sept. 18, claiming that they were repeatedly publishing “FAKE NEWS.” A day after his announcement, journalists from the outlets were turned away from the White House gates and their press badges were taken away.
Within days, the three outlets proceeded to sue the Trump Administration, arguing that the ban violated the First Amendment and their Fifth Amendment right to due process. In solidarity with the impacted outlets, the five broadcast networks that comprise the White House TV pool, which records and shares video footage of the President on a rotating basis, also temporarily suspended their coverage of Trump.
A federal judge on Sept. 24 issued a temporary restraining order against Trump’s ban, in effect for 14 days, and ordered the President to immediately restore the affected outlets’ access, finding that the ban “likely violated” their “constitutional due process rights.” Following that order, journalists from the three outlets were once again allowed to access the White House grounds.
But access to carry out pool duties has remained a point of contention. The White House previously blocked CNN from Air Force One, preventing the network from carrying out its scheduled TV pool duties.
POLITICO, CNN, and MS NOW, in response to CNN being prevented from traveling on the President’s plane and fulfilling its pool duties, previously requested that a federal judge block Trump’s ban on the outlets until their case against him was resolved, arguing that he had violated the previously implemented restraining order and had “persisted in unpredictably and inconsistently implementing its ban.”
“The White House’s words and actions leave little doubt that it will immediately reinstitute a complete ban of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO if allowed the opportunity,” the outlets’ lawyers wrote in a filing last week.
Judge Timothy J. Kelly of the U.S. District Court in Washington, who granted the temporary restraining order against the ban, is scheduled to hold a hearing over the outlets’ request to extend against Trump on Thursday.
The TV press pool has meanwhile resumed coverage of Trump after journalists from the outlets targeted in the ban were allowed back onto the White House grounds. But people familiar with the situation previously told TIME after CNN was blocked from traveling on Air Force One that decisions about TV pool coverage of the President would be made on a day-by-day basis amid the ongoing uncertainty over the network’s access to perform its pool duties.

sources.news_title: White House removes Politico from press pool for Trump’s trip to Nebraska
sources.text:
The White House prohibited Politico on Monday from traveling on Air Force One with President Donald Trump as he heads to Nebraska for a campaign rally.
The move comes amid a legal fight between the Trump administration and several news organizations.
“Many outlets including Politico are granted access to attend and cover presidential events unilaterally, but traveling with the President of the United States aboard Air Force One is a privilege not a right,” a White House official said in a statement.
CNN first reported the administration’s action against Politico.
The White House last month banned Politico, CNN and MS NOW from entering the White House, with Trump saying on Truth Social that the move was “a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” A federal judge last month ordered the administration to temporarily restore their access, but the order was limited to the White House grounds.
Dana Beckman, a spokesperson for Politico, confirmed that the news outlet was excluded from the travel pool but did not have additional comment. A lawyer representing the three news outlets in their lawsuit against the White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The White House last week removed CNN from the press pool set to cover Trump’s trip to Texas and Oklahoma.
The White House press pool consists of media outlets that share video, editorial information and costs for coverage of high-profile officials and events involving the president anywhere in the world. Under the system, designated “poolers” represent the wider press corps each day to document newsworthy events and serve as a conduit between the president and the public.

After CNN was restricted from administration events last month, the four other member networks of the press pool — Fox News, ABC News, CBS News and NBC News — declined to participate in pool duties in solidarity.
CBS on Monday said it would share its TV pool notes — which are usually distributed internally among the five pool networks — with the White House Correspondents’ Association. The network noted it was not replacing Politico as the print pool.
The White House Correspondents’ Association, the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press and a group of 49 news and media organizations that included NBCUniversal Media, the parent company of NBC News, filed a legal brief last month in support of CNN, MS NOW and Politico.

sources.news_title: Trump's press pool purge expands as Politico faces new Air Force One ban
sources.text:
The legal and political standoff between President Donald Trump’s administration and the White House press corps escalated Monday after Politico was blocked from traveling aboard Air Force One.
The move prevented the news organization from carrying out its scheduled duties as the designated print representative in the presidential travel pool, adding a new front to an increasingly contentious dispute over press access.
The administration’s decision comes as Trump’s White House faces legal challenges from several major news organizations over restrictions on access to presidential events and facilities, with press freedom and First Amendment protections at the center of the dispute.
"We can confirm that Politico was excluded from today’s out-of-town travel pool," a Politico spokesperson told Newsweek. "We do not have additional comment at this time, but would refer you back to our legal filings, previous statements and those from our attorney, Ted Boutrous."
The White House declined to comment when reached by Newsweek.
Full List of News Outlets Trump Has Blocked From the White House Press Pool
Politico, CNN and MS NOW
Trump announced on September 18 that Politico, CNN and MS NOW would be barred from the White House, accusing the outlets of publishing what he called “FAKE NEWS” and “FICTION and LIES.”
“I am proud to announce that, effective immediately, I am banning Fake News CNN, MSNOW … and Politico … from the White House as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
Trump did not provide evidence for his claims that the outlets had published false information.
The three outlets filed a joint lawsuit on September 21, arguing that the administration had violated their constitutional rights. In a joint statement, they said they were acting to “protect our First Amendment rights” and defend the principle that “the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes.” They also argued that the White House had revoked their journalists’ credentials “because it objected to our reporting.”
The lawsuit has developed into a broader fight over who controls access to the presidential press pool. Because space is limited at some presidential events and during travel, only a small number of reporters can attend in person and traditionally represent the broader White House press corps, sharing information with journalists who cannot be present.
U.S. District Judge Timothy J. Kelly subsequently ordered the administration to restore the outlets’ White House credentials while the lawsuit proceeds. The White House has maintained that restoring physical press credentials does not automatically give the outlets access to every restricted setting, including the Oval Office or Air Force One.
That argument was reinforced in a Justice Department filing on Friday in which the administration asked the court to allow Trump’s ban to stand. The government argued that Trump had determined the outlets published stories that “adversely affect national security” and that restricting their access would remove one avenue through which they could obtain information the administration considered harmful. The filing is part of the administration’s effort to defend the restrictions as the outlets seek a preliminary injunction.
The media organizations strongly dispute that argument. Ted Boutrous, the lead attorney representing CNN, MS NOW and Politico, told Newsweek that his legal team had already established that the ban was a “blatant violation of the First Amendment and due process.”
“Since then, the president has only made it clearer that he announced this ban to punish reporting he doesn’t like and try to force journalists to cover him in ways he prefers,” Boutrous said.
He said that the White House’s Friday filing showed that the president’s “ban on the free press” was “indefensible.”
“The law is absolutely clear. The harm to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound,” Boutrous said. “It is critical that the White House is enjoined to keep this unconstitutional ban on the free press out of commission.”
The dispute has continued even after Kelly’s order. CNN was excluded from several pool assignments in late September and early October, including presidential travel, prompting pushback from other members of the press corps. On Monday, the administration prevented Politico from boarding Air Force One for Trump’s trip to Nebraska, despite the outlet’s scheduled position as the print representative in the travel pool.
The administration has argued that the judge’s order restored general White House access but did not require officials to place the outlets in every limited-capacity event or presidential travel pool. White House Communications Director Steven Cheung said last week: “The judge basically ordered them to renew their access back to the White House, but that’s different than allowing the pool into the events in the Oval Office or on Air Force One.”
The case is scheduled for another significant hearing Thursday, when Kelly is expected to consider the outlets’ request for a preliminary injunction that would provide broader protection for their access while the lawsuit proceeds.
Other Outlets Decline Seat
Following Politico's exclusion from Monday's flight, the White House offered the vacant travel-pool position to other news organizations participating in the rotation.
Several publications declined the opportunity in solidarity with Politico and the other news organizations facing restrictions, sources familiar with the situation told CNN.
The White House's official Sunday night guidance email also notably omitted the names of news organizations traveling with Trump.
The unusual development underscored the reluctance among some members of the press corps to fill the seat left vacant after Politico was prevented from participating.
The incident is expected to be presented as additional evidence at a hearing Thursday, when Kelly is scheduled to consider the media organizations' request for a preliminary injunction.
The hearing could provide a significant test of the administration's interpretation of the existing court order and the broader question of how much discretion the White House has to determine which news organizations receive access to presidential travel and events.
The dispute comes amid a broader confrontation between the Trump administration and major news organizations over the role of the press in covering the presidency, with both sides offering sharply different interpretations of the constitutional and legal limits on restricting access.
The Associated Press
The Associated Press has faced a separate battle with the Trump administration over access to presidential events. The dispute began in February 2025 after the AP continued using the term "Gulf of Mexico" rather than Trump's preferred "Gulf of America."
The administration subsequently restricted AP journalists from certain limited-access events, including the Oval Office and Air Force One. The AP sued, arguing that the restrictions amounted to retaliation for its editorial decisions and violated the First Amendment. A federal judge later ruled that the AP was likely to prevail on its First Amendment claim and ordered the White House to restore its access while the case continued.
The administration appealed, arguing that the White House has broad authority to determine which journalists participate in events where space is limited. An appeals court allowed the restrictions to remain in place while the litigation continued. The AP case has since become an important backdrop to the newer dispute involving CNN, MS NOW and Politico, with both sides offering competing interpretations of how much control the White House has over limited press access and whether that authority can be used to exclude news organizations because of their coverage.
Reuters and HuffPost
Reuters and the Huffington Post have not faced the same blanket White House ban as the AP or the September restrictions imposed on CNN, MS NOW and Politico.
However, reporters for Reuters and the HuffPost were among those barred from covering Trump's first Cabinet meeting in February 2025. Reuters had been a longtime participant in the presidential press pool, while HuffPost had been scheduled to provide the print pool reporter that day before being removed and replaced by another outlet.
Reuters and the AP also objected to the administration's decision to take control of pool assignments from the White House Correspondents' Association, arguing that limiting the number of wire services with access could reduce the distribution of independent, real-time information about the presidency.
More significantly, in April 2025, the White House eliminated the permanent wire-service position in the press pool. The change affected Reuters, AP and Bloomberg, which had traditionally occupied dedicated wire-service positions. Under the new system, wire services could still be selected for the pool but no longer had a guaranteed place. Reuters said it remained committed to covering the White House accurately and independently.
Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gabe Whisnant and Dave Siminoff.

sources.news_title: Trump Blocks Politico From Air Force One After Requesting Judge Reinstate Media Ban
Politico Blocked From Air Force One In Latest Trump White House Effort To Punish Media Over Reporting
sources.text:
The White House blocked Politico from traveling with Donald Trump on Air Force One on Monday for the president’s trip to Nebraska.
A Politico spokesperson confirmed that the publication was excluded from the out-of-town travel pool, the handful of reporters who cover the president’s travel with each outlet assigned on a rotating basis. The Washington Post was providing reports as the secondary print pooler, but the White House did not find a replacement for Politico, according to a member of the pool.
The exclusion of Politico comes after Trump banned the publication, along with CNN and MS NOW, from the White House grounds on Sept. 18. But a federal judge ruled that the administration failed to provide due process, and ordered that hard passes to dozens of reporters be restored. The judge’s order expires later this week, and the three outlets are seeking a preliminary injunction to sideline the ban in the longer term. A hearing is scheduled for Thursday.
Since then, the White House also has banned CNN from Air Force One travel and other events.
Watch on Deadline
The Trump administration restrictions on access to certain areas of the White House grounds is a separate but related issue. White House officials have argued that they can freeze out media from certain areas like the Oval Office, as well as spaces like Air Force One, even when the reason has to do with what stories an outlet publishes or reports. In a separate case, the Associated Press has been challenging those restrictions, arguing that it violates the First Amendment as a form of viewpoint discrimination. The case is on appeal.
A White House official said, “Many outlets including Politico are granted access to attend and cover presidential events unilaterally, but traveling with the President of the United States aboard Air Force One is a privilege not a right. President Trump is the most accessible President in American history — holding open press events, taking unfiltered questions directly from the media almost every day, and posting directly to his TRUTH Social account — and he will continue to grant an unprecedented level of access to the press.”
The DOJ argued in a court filing on Friday that, in restricting CNN and other outlets from the White House grounds, the president made a determination that they did not meet “minimum requirements of professionalism,” citing reporting on national security information and other stories.
CNN first reported on the ban on Politico from the pool.

sources.news_title: White House Blocks Politico From Traveling On Air Force One
sources.text:
The White House on Monday refused to allow a Politico reporter aboard Air Force One on the president’s trip to Grand Island, Nebraska.
Politico confirmed to HuffPost that the outlet had been scheduled to provide out-of-town pool coverage but declined to comment further.
The decision represents an escalation in President Donald Trump’s war on the First Amendment. Last month, the White House similarly left CNN off Air Force One even though it had been scheduled to provide independent media coverage of Trump’s visit to Tennessee; instead, a far-right outlet tagged along for fawning coverage.
“FAKE NEWS SHOULD NOT BE ALLOWED IN THE WHITE HOUSE!!! IT HAS GONE ON FAR TOO LONG, AT A TREMENDOUS COST TO OUR COUNTRY,” Trump wrote on social media at the time.
One of the purported “fake” stories that triggered Trump was an accurate report that Florida gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds had removed references to Trump from his website.
In September, a federal judge ordered the Trump administration to restore access to journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico after Trump attempted to ban them from the White House. The order, however, didn’t specifically address pool duties or Air Force One.
The White House leaned heavily on that omission while attempting to explain Politico’s ejection.
“Many outlets including Politico are granted access to attend and cover presidential events unilaterally, but traveling with the President of the United States aboard Air Force One is a privilege not a right,” a spokesperson told HuffPost.
Trump said on social media at the time that he’d done so because he thought they “constantly write or report FICTION and LIES,” only to later claim he’d kicked them out over a vague claim related to national security.
U.S. District Judge Tim Kelly, a Trump appointee, didn’t buy the national security argument and ordered the White House to immediately return their press passes, saying it “likely violated their constitutional due process rights.”

sources.text:
White House bans Politico from Air Force One in latest Trump attack on media
Trump administration continues to block reporters from covering the president during legal battle over press access

The White House has blocked Politico from covering Donald Trump on Air Force One, stopping the media outlet from traveling with the president to cover the administration as part of a small group of correspondents that follow him out of town.
A spokesperson for Politico confirmed to The Independent that the White House excluded the outlet from Monday’s out-of-town travel pool. CNN first reported the ban.
The move comes days after a federal judge ordered the administration to restore press passes that belonged to several journalists from CNN, Politico and MS NOW, which the president said he was “banning” from the White House, likely in violation of the First and Fifth Amendments.
But reporters from CNN, and now Politico, have continued to be barred from Air Force One on days their outlets have been assigned to provide print or television coverage of the president’s travel.
Administration officials have sought to distinguish the removal of individual outlets and reporters from the White House, which a judge has rejected, to pool coverage on Air Force One. Last week, in an interview with TIME, Trump denied that he was violating the court order while White House communications director Steven Cheung said restoring press passes is “different than allowing the pool into the events in the Oval Office or on Air Force One.”
The White House told The Independent that traveling on Air Force One is a “privilege not a right” and defended Trump has “the most accessible President in American history” who “will continue to grant an unprecedented level of access to the press.”
U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly is set to bring the parties back to his courtroom Thursday to determine whether to grant a preliminary injunction that would prevent the White House from stripping press access while the legal challenge is ongoing.
In a ruling granting a temporary restraining order last month, Kelly rejected the government’s arguments that the president’s ban was motivated by national security concerns.
“The record lacks factual support for defendants’ contention that the revocation of plaintiffs’ hard passes will in fact protect national security or that national security will be endangered if the court orders their passes reinstated while this litigation proceeds,” Kelly wrote.
In court filings, lawyers for the media outlets argue that the president’s actions “leave little doubt” that he will try to “immediately” impose a “complete ban” on their coverage unless the courts intervene.
The administration’s attempts to justify the ban, days after implementing it, are merely “weapons for the arbitrary and discriminatory enforcement that due process forbids,” lawyers wrote last week.
The Department of Justice, meanwhile, has argued that the outlets failed to meet “minimum requirements of professionalism.”
Government lawyers wrote Friday that there is “no basis” for the court to grant them “full access to all areas of the White House” and other sensitive areas.
The outlets don’t have a “First Amendment right to these areas,” according to the Justice Department.
In an order that arrived around 1 a.m. September 24, Kelly required the White House to reinstate the outlets’ credentials and restore their access to the White House grounds, but it did not explicitly address their participation in the pool coverage.
Reporters from the three outlets were denied entry to the White House on the morning of September 24, despite Kelly’s order, but were allowed inside White House grounds around noon.
The following day, CNN learned that it would not be permitted to travel aboard Air Force One as the designated television network pooler for the president’s trip to Knoxville, Tennessee, according to the outlet’s lawyers.
“CNN received no official communication from the White House explaining its exclusion,” they wrote. “Because CNN was excluded and no replacement designated, no primary television network pooler accompanied the President on the trip.”
Judge Kelly’s temporary restraining order is set to expire October 8, the same day that the parties will convene for another court hearing in Washington, D.C.
Unless the judge issues a preliminary injunction, which will last through the duration of the legal battle ahead of a potential trial, harms against the press “will quickly compound,” lawyers wrote.

sources.news_title: White House Blocks Politico From Air Force One Amid Ongoing Press Access Lawsuit
sources.text:
The White House barred Politico from traveling aboard Air Force One on Monday despite a federal judge’s order restoring the outlet’s White House credentials, sharpening a legal dispute over whether access to the president’s traveling press pool is covered by the same constitutional protections.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom.
WASHINGTON — The White House blocked Politico from traveling aboard Air Force One on Monday, preventing the publication from serving as the designated print pool representative on President Donald Trump’s trip to Nebraska as a broader court fight over presidential press access continues.
A Politico spokesperson confirmed that the publication was excluded from the out-of-town travel pool, the small rotating group of reporters assigned to accompany the president and share information with the wider White House press corps.
The exclusion came less than two weeks after U.S. District Judge Timothy J. Kelly ordered the administration to restore White House press credentials to Politico, CNN and MS NOW following Trump’s Sept. 18 announcement that he was banning the three outlets from White House access.
The three news organizations sued Sept. 21, alleging that the administration violated the First and Fifth Amendments by revoking access because of their coverage.
Kelly granted a temporary restraining order Sept. 24 requiring the administration to reinstate the journalists’ White House credentials for 14 days.
The judge concluded that the outlets had shown a likelihood of success on their Fifth Amendment procedural due-process claim and found that the government had offered little evidence that the ban was genuinely based on national-security concerns.
The ruling, however, did not expressly resolve a separate question now at the center of the dispute: whether restoring a journalist’s White House credential also requires the administration to include that outlet in restricted-capacity presidential events or on Air Force One.
The White House has taken the position that it does not.
Communications Director Steven Cheung said last week that the court order restored access to the White House complex but did not necessarily guarantee participation in the rotating press pool.
“The judge basically ordered them to renew their access back to the White House, but that’s different than allowing the pool into the events in the Oval Office or on Air Force One,” Cheung said.
That distinction has already affected CNN.
Since Kelly issued his order, the White House has repeatedly prevented CNN from performing its scheduled role as television pool representative on Air Force One, according to reporting on the case.
Politico’s exclusion Monday extended that dispute to the print pool.
Under longstanding White House press arrangements, pool reporters serve a broader function than ordinary individual coverage.
Because space around the president is frequently limited, selected reporters, photographers and television crews rotate through events and travel assignments and distribute their observations, quotes and other information to the larger press corps.
Politico had been scheduled to fill the print role during Monday’s trip.
By preventing its reporter from boarding Air Force One, the White House also prevented the publication from carrying out that scheduled pool responsibility.
It was not immediately clear which outlet, if any, replaced Politico in that role.
The administration has not publicly explained Monday’s decision in detail.
Trump announced Sept. 18 that Politico, CNN and MS NOW would no longer be permitted at the White House, accusing the organizations of false reporting.
The administration subsequently argued in court that the restrictions were justified in part by national-security concerns.
Kelly, a Trump appointee, questioned that explanation.
In his order, the judge wrote that nothing in the record predating the lawsuit indicated that national security had actually motivated the credential revocations.
“For one thing, nothing in the record that predates this suit suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes was motivated by national security concerns,” Kelly wrote.
The judge did not make a final ruling on all of the outlets’ constitutional claims.
Instead, he temporarily restored their credentials while the lawsuit proceeds.
The outlets are now asking Kelly for a preliminary injunction that would preserve their access for a longer period while the case moves toward a potential trial.
A hearing on that request is scheduled for Thursday.
Ted Boutrous, an attorney representing CNN, MS NOW and Politico, said the dispute involves fundamental press protections.
“The law is absolutely clear. The harm to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound,” Boutrous said.
“It is critical that the White House is enjoined to keep this unconstitutional ban on the free press out of commission.”
The administration disputes the outlets’ interpretation of the law and has defended the president’s authority to determine access to limited spaces and presidential events.
That argument raises a legal question distinct from whether the government may revoke an otherwise valid White House credential without due process.
The Supreme Court has not directly established that every credentialed reporter has a constitutional right to travel aboard Air Force One or attend every limited-capacity presidential event.
But federal courts have recognized due-process protections once the government establishes a system of White House press credentials.
That precedent traces in part to Sherrill v. Knight, a 1977 decision from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit requiring the government to apply clear standards and procedural protections before denying White House press access.
The Trump administration has indicated in the current litigation that it wants courts to reconsider parts of that nearly 50-year-old precedent.
The dispute also resembles an ongoing lawsuit involving The Associated Press.
The White House restricted AP access to certain presidential events and spaces after the news organization continued referring to the Gulf of Mexico by that name following Trump’s executive order directing the federal government to use “Gulf of America.”
The AP challenged those restrictions in federal court, arguing the government could not penalize a news organization based on editorial choices.
That litigation likewise raised the distinction between holding general White House credentials and obtaining access to smaller presidential events where space is controlled by the administration.
The latest conflict began when Trump publicly singled out CNN, MS NOW and Politico in September.
The outlets responded by suing the president and administration officials, arguing that the restrictions amounted to retaliation for protected reporting and that journalists received no adequate notice or opportunity to challenge the decision before losing access.
Kelly’s temporary order restored their hard passes, and the White House eventually allowed the reporters back onto White House grounds.
There was initially further friction after the order was issued.
Reporters from all three organizations were briefly denied entry despite the court’s ruling, prompting the outlets to seek an emergency hearing.
The White House later said the credentials had been restored and were available for pickup, and the journalists returned to the complex.
The travel-pool dispute remained unresolved.
CNN, MS NOW and Politico returned to court Sept. 29 seeking a longer-lasting injunction against the administration’s restrictions.
They argue that restoring a physical credential while excluding their journalists from important parts of presidential coverage leaves significant portions of the original ban effectively intact.
The administration argues that entry to the White House complex and participation in the pool are separate decisions.
Monday’s treatment of Politico brings that disagreement into sharper focus.
A reporter with a restored credential can enter the White House, but under the administration’s current position, the president may still deny that outlet a seat on Air Force One or access to a limited event even when the outlet is scheduled to serve as the pool representative.
The courts have not yet issued a final answer on whether that distinction is legally sustainable in the circumstances of this case.
The consequences extend beyond the three organizations involved.
The White House Correspondents’ Association relies on rotating pools so reporters who cannot physically accompany the president can still receive timely information about his statements, movements and activities.
Limiting a scheduled pool outlet therefore affects not only that organization’s own reporting but also information distributed to other members of the press.
Politico’s exclusion occurred as Trump traveled Monday to Nebraska for a campaign appearance.
The president has increasingly returned to the campaign trail ahead of the November midterm elections, making presidential travel coverage especially significant during the final weeks before voting.
The White House has not indicated how long Politico’s exclusion from Air Force One will continue.
Kelly is expected to consider the larger issue when he hears arguments Thursday on the outlets’ request for a preliminary injunction.
That hearing could determine whether the administration may continue drawing a distinction between general White House access and participation in the traveling and event pools while the lawsuit proceeds.
For now, Politico’s credentials have been restored under court order.
Its seat aboard Air Force One has not.

The White House blocked Politico from traveling aboard Air Force One on Monday, preventing the outlet from carrying out its scheduled duties in the presidential press pool amid an ongoing legal fight with the Trump administration.
Politico was set to serve as the out-of-town print pool reporter for President Donald Trump’s trip to Nebraska, but was excluded from the traveling press group, a spokesperson for the outlet confirmed to TheWrap.
The exclusion underscores the limits of the outlets’ recent court victory: CNN, MS NOW and Politico regained access to the White House grounds last month, but the administration has continued restricting their participation in limited-capacity presidential events, including on Air Force One.
The White House repeatedly blocked CNN from Air Force One when the network was scheduled to serve as the television pool representative.
Trump announced last month that he was barring the three outlets from the White House, prompting CNN, MS NOW and Politico to sue the administration. The three organizations regained access to the White House grounds hours after the ruling following another court standoff.
The temporary order applies to access to the White House complex, while the administration has argued that it does not extend to limited-capacity spaces such as Air Force One or the Oval Office.

sources.text:
The White House refused to allow Politico to travel with President Donald Trump aboard Air Force One on Monday, a spokesperson for the outlet said.
Politico is part of a trio of news companies, along with CNN and MS NOW, that Trump banned from the White House on Sept. 18, and several journalists had their media passes confiscated when they tried to enter the grounds. Judge Timothy J. Kelly issued a temporary restraining order on the policy on Sept. 24 and directed the White House to reinstate the journalists’ passes.
Politico confirmed that the outlet had been excluded from the out-of-town travel pool on Monday, despite Kelly’s order. The outlet was slated to be the print pool representative on Monday. CNN first reported the news.
CNN had also been blocked from fulfilling its pool duties on the days the network was assigned to be the TV pool representative.
Trending
Trump is set to travel to Nebraska for a campaign stop in Grand Island.
The White House defended its decision in a statement to The Washington Sun, saying that “Trump is the most accessible President in American history” because of the frequency with which he appears in front of reporters and the fact that he posts often on social media.
“Many outlets including Politico are granted access to attend and cover presidential events unilaterally, but traveling with the President of the United States aboard Air Force One is a privilege not a right,” a White House spokesperson added.
White House Communications Director Steven Cheung previously said he believes that Kelly’s order restoring access to the White House grounds does not cover journalists’ ability to cover the president through pool events.
“The judge basically ordered them to renew their access back to the White House, but that’s different than allowing the pool into the events in the Oval Office or on Air Force One,” Cheung told TIME on Sept. 28 during the outlet’s interview with the president.
In his order, Kelly cited due process concerns spurred by the White House confiscating journalists’ badges without prior notice or an appropriate opportunity to be heard regarding the decision.
But Kelly’s order did not specify whether the White House can legally ban journalists conducting their pool duties, which are agreements in which a rotating group of journalists cover an event or political figure and share material and information with the wider press corps. Journalists covering Trump may have to execute their pool responsibilities within the White House grounds, or they can work through a travel pool if the president has a scheduled trip.
Kelly’s temporary restraining order expires Thursday. Attorneys for the media outlets filed a motion on Sept. 28 urging Kelly to issue a preliminary injunction to block the ban while the case proceeds in court. Kelly has not issued a ruling on the media outlet’s request, but a hearing is scheduled Thursday to review the motion.
“The White House has persisted in unpredictably and inconsistently implementing its ban, including by barring CNN from fulfilling its role as designated television network pooler on September 26—to the detriment of CNN, its fellow pool members and, ultimately, the American public,” the filing from media outlets reads.

sources.text:
White House blocks Politico from Air Force One amid press access lawsuit
By Brian Stelter, CNN
(CNN) — The White House is refusing to allow Politico on Air Force One on Monday, which means the news organization cannot fulfill its press corps pool responsibilities.
A Politico spokesperson confirmed that the publication was excluded from the out-of-town travel pool, a small group of reporters who travel with the president on trips.
The White House tried to enlist other news outlets to take Politico’s place on the trip, but “it was unable to find a replacement,” so “there is no primary print pooler on this trip,” Washington Post reporter Katherine Doyle said in an email to colleagues.
The Post is on the trip in the “secondary” print seat as part of the pool. The “secondary” reporter does not typically send out updates to the wider press corps. But with Trump traveling to Nebraska for a campaign stop on Monday afternoon, The Post is sending out updates while emphasizing that it is not taking Politico’s place.
The television press pool representative on Monday, CBS, is also sharing its pool notes with print publications during the trip, given the unusual circumstances.
“Neither news organization is replacing Politico,” Josh Gross of CBS News wrote in an internal email.
Monday’s moves amount to another show of solidarity by news outlets that usually compete fiercely on the White House beat.
The White House offered Politico’s seat to many other news organizations that routinely take turns in the oawut-of-town travel pool, and the publications uniformly declined, sources with knowledge of the matter told CNN.
President Donald Trump announced on September 18 that he was “banning” Politico, CNN and MS NOW from the White House, a move that legal experts called unconstitutional.
The news outlets filed a lawsuit on September 21 alleging the ban violates the First and Fifth Amendments. Judge Timothy J. Kelly sided with the plaintiffs and issued a temporary restraining order requiring the Trump administration to reinstate the journalists’ press badges.
Since then, however, the White House has repeatedly barred CNN from traveling on Air Force One on days when it has been CNN’s turn to be the TV pool representative. Now, on the day it was Politico’s turn to be the print pool representative, Politico has been barred as well.
The Trump administration appears to be justifying these new restrictions by saying that access to the White House complex is different than access to tight spaces like Air Force One. The Associated Press has an ongoing lawsuit over this distinction, since Trump tried to ban the wire service from certain spaces last year.
Monday’s action against Politico will likely be incorporated into the next legal filing by CNN, MS NOW and Politico.
“The law is absolutely clear. The harm to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound,” the attorney for the three news outlets, Ted Boutrous, said in a statement. “It is critical that the White House is enjoined to keep this unconstitutional ban on the free press out of commission.”
Last week, when reporters from TIME asked if Trump was ignoring the court order, Trump said no, and then communications director Steven Cheung piped in: “The judge basically ordered them to renew their access back to the White House, but that’s different than allowing the pool into the events in the Oval Office or on Air Force One.”
When asked about the action against Politico on Monday, a White House spokesperson told CNN, “Many outlets including Politico are granted access to attend and cover presidential events unilaterally, but traveling with the President of the United States aboard Air Force One is a privilege not a right.”
That’s what Trump’s Justice Department is also arguing in court.
Judge Kelly is scheduled to hold a hearing on Thursday over the news outlets’ request for a preliminary injunction, which would protect press access to the White House for a longer period of time ahead of a potential trial.
The White House spokesperson asserted that Trump “will continue to grant an unprecedented level of access to the press.”
His recent actions, however, show a desire to pick and choose who asks questions and documents his presidency.
This story has been updated with additional details.

Trump Is Still Banning News Outlets From Air Force One
But some media organizations are pushing back.
Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images
The White House continued its press ban Monday, blocking the news outlet Politico from traveling on Air Force One with President Trump.
Politico was scheduled to be the White House print pool representative, and Trump administration officials offered its spot on the plane to other news organizations who are part of the pool. In solidarity, several print organizations said no, CNN reports.
The night before, the White House’s email to the press corps offering guidance on Trump’s trip did not mention any news outlets who were traveling on Air Force One, which is not normal, and could be a sign that media organizations are trying to send a message to the president. Last month, Trump banned MS NOW, Politico, and CNN from the White House, only to be rebuked by U.S. District Court Judge Timothy Kelly, who ordered the ban immediately lifted while the outlets’ court challenge received a full hearing.
At the time, the rest of the White House TV pool refused to cover Chinese President Xi Jinping’s arrival at the White House, leaving only Chinese state media to have video of Xi’s entrance September 24. At the state dinner for Xi that same night, a dumbfounded Trump asked where all of the cameras were.
In an interview with Time magazine published last week, Trump appeared to be confused about Kelly’s order and is still bent on punishing news outlets for coverage that he doesn’t like. The fact that other mainstream media outlets aren’t trying to take advantage of Trump’s ban to get increased access to the president is a good sign. Enabling Trump’s latest attacks on the press would result in watered-down, less critical news coverage of a president who thinks he is above any laws or checks on his power.
Another MAGA Candidate Scrubs Mentions of Trump From His Website
Georgia gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson apparently doesn’t want to seem so close to Donald Trump anymore.
Georgia Republican gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson
Elijah Nouvelage/Getty Images
Georgia Republican gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson
Rick Jackson, the Republican gubernatorial nominee in Georgia, is the latest MAGA candidate to delete mentions of President Donald Trump from his campaign website.
A version of Jackson’s website from June stated that he “will work with President Trump to protect Georgians from the consequences of Washington’s failures.” As of Monday, the mention had been removed, MeidasTouch reported.
This sudden deletion (read: defection) comes after Jackson spent months tirelessly tying himself to Trump. In February, his campaign aired a 30-second Super Bowl commercial comparing him to the president. “Like President Trump, I don’t owe anybody anything,” Jackson said. On the campaign trail, Jackson promised voters he’d be Trump’s “favorite governor,” and framed himself as similar to Trump, but with a “southern tone.”
All of this was done without Trump ever actually endorsing Jackson. The president reluctantly bestowed his endorsement to Jackson in July, after the businessman defeated Trump’s original pick, Lieutenant Governor Burt Jones, in the Republican primary runoff in June.
Jackson’s sudden switch-up is part of a wider trend of Republicans toning down their ties to the president ahead of the midterm elections. Jackson is at least the second candidate to remove Trump from his campaign website, after Florida Representative and gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds. The shift appears to indicate that the Republicans’ leader has become the party’s biggest liability.
Trump Had a Practice Run for Iran. He Messed It Up Too.
The Trump administration’s handling of Houthi militias presaged in 2025 many of its failures in Iran and the Strait of Hormuz a year later.
Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
President Trump’s ill-advised, poorly executed war in Iran was foreshadowed months before.
The Washington Postreports that the Trump administration’s handling of Yemen’s Houthi militia attacking ships in the area in 2025 had Pentagon leaders raising concerns that would come to fruition during the Iran war the next year.
Specifically, Department of Defense officials Dan Caldwell and Alex Velez-Green were worried that an extended military campaign against the Houthis could deplete U.S. missile stocks, which ended up happening one year later. Last year, in March 2025, President Trump announced Operation Rough Rider, a bombing campaign in Yemen that would become infamous after the national security adviser at the time, Mike Waltz, mistakenly invited Atlantic editor Jeffrey Goldberg into a group chat of senior administration officials discussing the early bombings.
The campaign resulted in 1,000 targets being bombed, with Houthi commanders and ammunition stocks being targeted, but also scores of civilians being killed. Trump and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth called the operation a success, but others in the Pentagon, such as Caldwell and Hegseth’s first chief of staff, Joe Kasper, questioned whether the operation had clear and achievable objectives, again similar to the current Iran war.
A spokesperson for Hegseth, Kingsley Wilson, told the Post that the operation “achieved decisive success against Houthi forces,” resulting in “severely degraded radar networks, air-defense systems, ballistic-missile and drone launch sites, weapons depots, and production facilities while removing multiple mid- and senior-level commanders from the battlefield.” It also “substantially reduced immediate threats to vital international shipping lanes, compelled a clear tactical shift by the adversary, and helped create conditions for a ceasefire that strengthened freedom of navigation in the region.”
Those “successes” seem at best hollow now, as Houthi forces took over the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait in the Red Sea last month. Last year’s operation ended in May 2025 with an Oman-brokered ceasefire and Trump declaring victory, claiming that the Houthis “don’t want to fight anymore.”
“They gave us their word that they wouldn’t be shooting at ships anymore, and we honor that,” Trump said.
In reality, the Houthis weathered the U.S. attacks. They shot down at least seven MQ-9 Reaper drones, and two F/A-18 fighter jets were lost at sea. Trump lost interest in Yemen shortly afterward, to the chagrin of some in U.S. Central Command. Some officials reportedly said at the time, “You ignore Yemen at your own peril.”
That seems all too apparent today, and the U.S. is stuck in a conflict with Iran and its Houthi allies with no clear end in sight. The war has stretched on and continues to hurt the U.S. and global economies, with Trump unwilling to acknowledge that the war should never been waged, was horribly executed, and now needs to end regardless of how bad he looks.
Trump Finds a New Way to Blame Gas Prices on Anyone But Himself
Sure, let’s blame another country that’s at war.
Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images
Suddenly, gas prices have absolutely nothing to do with the Iran war, according to the U.S. president.
After spending months denying and downplaying the fact that gas and diesel prices have become more expensive, Donald Trump finally conceded Monday. The only catch to his admission: The rising price tag is definitely not his fault.
“What’s driving up Gasoline is no longer the Strait of Hormuz, because Record Numbers of Barrels are coming out now on an almost daily basis,” Trump wrote on Truth Social Monday.
Instead, Trump blamed the sky-high prices on Ukraine, claiming that its recent attacks on Russian oil refineries had aggrieved the global oil market. (It’s worth noting that Ukraine would likely stop attacking Russian infrastructure if Trump’s buddy Russian President Vladimir Putin stopped invading Ukraine.) Trump also wagged a finger at “Blue States like California” that are trying to veer away from fossil fuels in favor of renewable energy sources.
Provisional ship-tracking data obtained by Reuters revealed that, in the last month of September, oil trade through the Strait of Hormuz had roughly returned to prewar levels. Millions of barrels of oil from European reserves are also expected to help lower prices in the near future, following an urgent plea from Trump to G7 leaders last week.
But American wallets are still hurting. The price of oil and gas has gone up exponentially since the start of the Iran war and the subsequent closure of the Strait of Hormuz. In early February, weeks before the Trump administration initiated the conflict, gas cost approximately $2.99 per gallon. Today, a gallon costs $4.36 on average, according to the AAA fuel price tracker.
This time last year, diesel cost an average of $3.68 a gallon, according to AAA. Today, it costs $6.32 a gallon.
Collectively, Americans have spent $107 billion more on gas and oil since the war began seven months ago, according to an analysis by the Climate Solutions Lab at Brown University published last month.
Consumers have spent roughly $59 billion more on gas and $48.6 billion more on diesel, according to the university’s tracker. That breaks down to an increased price tag of approximately $822.20 per U.S. household.
JD Vance Says Trump’s Weird Midterm Ads Are “Not Partisan”
Donald Trump has used taxpayer money to fund a series of ads touting himself and attacking Democrats.
Vice President JD Vance
Jacquelyn Martin/Getty Images
Vice President JD Vance
Vice President JD Vance claimed Monday that Donald Trump’s taxpayer-funded propaganda videos are actually “not partisan.”
The Trump administration has used at least 5.6 million taxpayer dollars to buy a series of at least 15 campaign-style advertisements touting the president’s agenda ahead of November’s midterm elections—even though it’s illegal to use government funds for campaign purposes.
Speaking to the press ahead of his trip to Alaska, Vance tried to downplay the administration’s blatant law-breaking by claiming the television spots did not endorse any particular candidate or party.
“I’m sure that some people don’t like it, but if you look at the message of those advertisements, they’re not partisan, they’re not—you know, it’s not like we’re advocating for a particular candidate,” Vance said. “We’re trying to tell a story, I think, about how great the United States of America is.”
The vice president compared the advertisements to videos that the Obama administration produced about the Affordable Care Act. “You have the people’s government using tax dollars to advertise about what the government is doing,” Vance continued. “It’s part of actually, I think, living in the constitutional republic.”
In 2010, the Department of Health and Human services paid to produce short 30-second ads explaining the changes that the Affordable Care Act made to Medicare, including free check-ups, cancer screenings, and lower prescription drug costs. Not only did these videos have a clear public service function, but they were also not self-aggrandizing or partisan.
By comparison, Trump’s television spots are wildly partisan. One spot, called “King of the Jungle,” features images of Democrats targeted by the Trump administration edited alongside videos of lions hunting in the wild. Another, called “God Made Trump,” presents the president as a messianic figure. One ad called “Resilience” shows multiple moments in Trump’s life before he became president. And in another, the president begs voters to “Love Me.”
In order to make the videos, the Trump administration stole the money from the Department of Homeland Security, specifically from U.S. Customs and Border Protection.

sources.text:
CNN host Jake Tapper completely embarrassed himself on live television by begging top Trump administration official, Ambassador Mike Waltz, to let the network come back on Air Force One after President Donald Trump gave them, Politico, and MS NOW the boot from White House grounds and from doing any sort of interviews with him.
The groveling was cut into a clip and posted on social media and it truly is pathetic to watch. “Sir, I just want to note. Yesterday, the White House barred CNN from fulfilling our pool assignment on behalf of the five major television networks. As you know, we all pool coverage, and all of our affiliates and subscribers. And I would just ask if you could please convey to President Trump to let CNN back in the pool. It was not okay when President Obama tried to freeze Fox out of the pool back in 2009, and I don’t think we want a world where presidents decide who gets to cover them,” he told Waltz.
The begging did not have the effect that Tapper was hoping for. “Well, I hear you, Jake, but I think we need fair and objective and well-sourced reporting, and I can tell you, as having been the victim of a lot of this nonsense, my family members, and so many others. “And whether that is Biden’s inability or the many issues that he had that were whitewashed, and then people came back around with corrections or other issues. So that’s a much longer conversation, and President Trump’s frustrated. By the way, there are over what 50 seats in the press room,” Waltz continued.
“I don’t think all of them, like Washington Post or New York Times, are exactly positive towards this administration, so that’s a false narrative that is about negative reporting. We need fair and objective reporting for the country, and that’s President Trump’s point,” Waltz explained to both Tapper and the viewing audience.
Tapper then fired back, saying the president said there’s something wrong with a country that allows people to report things that are purposely negative, pointing out this was the language Trump used, not his own. “Well, I think he’s going to what I just said in that there is a negative agenda, there is a negative narrative, and then we’re going to get anonymous sources,” Waltz answered.
"*" indicates required fields
“Heck, I just saw a story where anonymous sources were referring to a now dead senator,” Waltz told Tapper. The CNN host then said, “So this needs to be fixed, and President Trump is quite frustrated with this media bias across the board. As has every single president that I’ve ever covered been frustrated with the press. But Ambassador Waltz, I appreciate your time today. Thank you so much for joining us. Thank you.”
